questions.question: How do you handle an interview question you don't know?
questions.title: Handling Unknown Questions
questions.direct_answer: When you don't know an answer, don't fake it — say 'I'm not certain, but here's how I'd find out', then reason from what you DO know. Interviewers test honesty and problem-solving, not memorization; a confident 'I don't know, but I'd check the docs / write a test / ask a senior' beats a wrong guess. If it's a coding question, talk through what you'd try (edge cases, a simpler version, the docs). The trap to avoid is freezing, guessing wrong and confidently, or pretending you know — all signal worse than an honest 'I'd look it up'.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you say 'I don't know, but here's how I'd find out' and reason from what you do know (honesty + process).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freezing, or guessing confidently and wrong — both worse than an honest 'I'd look it up'.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Say 'I'm not certain, but here's how I'd find out'; reason from what you know. Interviewers test honesty + process, not memorization.

sections.title: Honesty Beats a Wrong Guess
sections.content: When you don't know an answer, don't fake it — say 'I'm not certain, but here's how I'd find out', then reason from what you DO know. Interviewers test honesty and problem-solving, not memorization; a confident 'I don't know, but I'd check the docs, write a test, or ask a senior' beats a wrong guess. If it's a coding question, talk through what you'd try — the edge cases, a simpler version, the docs. The trap to avoid is freezing, guessing wrong and confidently, or pretending you know — all signal worse than an honest 'I'd look it up', because the interviewer already knows the answer and is watching how you handle not knowing.

sections.title: Unknown -> Honest Reasoning
sections.content:
Say 'I don't know'; then show your process (docs, test, simpler version).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Q[question you don't know] --> A['I'm not certain, but...']
  A --> R[reason from what you know]
  R --> P[state how you'd find out: docs/test/senior]
```

sections.title: How to phrase it
sections.content:
```ruby
# Good responses when you don't know:

# 'I'm not 100% sure of the exact method, but I'd check the Rails docs —
#  I'd look for the query methods, since where and order return a Relation.'

# 'I haven't used that gem, but based on how Sidekiq works, I'd expect a worker
#  class and a perform method; I'd read its README to confirm.'

# 'I don't know that one offhand. If I hit it at work, I'd write a tiny test,
#  reproduce it, and check the stack trace.'

# Avoid:
#   * Freezing silently.
#   * 'I think it's...' (confident wrong guess).
```

sections.title: Responses Ranked
rows: 'I'd check the docs / write a test / ask.'

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Freezing silently — say something; even 'let me think' buys time.
Guessing confidently and wrong — the interviewer knows; it looks worse than 'I'd look it up'.
Pretending you know and getting caught — trust is gone for the rest of the interview.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Don't fake it — say 'I'm not certain, but here's how I'd find out'.
Interviewers test honesty + process, not memorization.
Reason from what you DO know (similar tools, how things work).
State how you'd find out: check docs, write a test, ask a senior.
Avoid freezing and confident wrong guesses — both signal worse than honesty.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: When you don't know an answer, don't fake it — say I'm not certain, but here's how I'd find out, then reason from what you do know. Interviewers test honesty and problem-solving, not memorization; a confident I don't know, but I'd check the docs, write a test, or ask a senior beats a wrong guess. If it's a coding question, talk through what you'd try — the edge cases, a simpler version, the docs. The trap to avoid is freezing, guessing wrong and confidently, or pretending you know, all of which signal worse than an honest I'd look it up, because the interviewer already knows the answer and is watching how you handle not knowing. A confident wrong guess is the worst, because the interviewer knows and it looks worse than admitting it.
